SHIPPING SHAMBLES

By: Nicky Troll | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
DISRUPTIONS IN WORLD TRADE triggered by war create a golden opportunity for South Africa to boost its own economy - but ironically it’s an opportunity the country is missing out on. SUMMARY

Unique Selling Point:
A WAR STORY WITHOUT IT BEING ABOUT WAR

Summary:
In any war there is collateral damage, direct and indirect economic impact and ironically even opportunities for some to benefit.

Right now, global trade is being disrupted as attacks in the Red Sea hots up, with shipping companies vowing to avoid those waters rerouting ships thousands of miles away around the Cape of Good Hope.

It could be a golden opportunity for South Africa - but it’s not. We ask why.



Further information:
WHY TELL THIS STORY?
This is a way to do a story about the war, without doing a story about war and making relevant to South Africa
HOW WE TELL THIS STORY
We set the scene - the war in Gaza, the attacks in Yemen using visuals of the attacks. Then we demonstrate the ripple effect on the shipping industry using maps and graphics.
This is our springboard into looking at the current crisis at South African ports and the red tape that’s causing the country to lose out on potentially very lucrative opportunity to benefit from war.
We take it up a notch by including transnet / shipping industry insider that will act a as a deep throat - explaining the shortcomings of a port system broken by ineffective management, a lack of resources and of course corruption (dealt with in broad strokes - no crazy RORs)

BACKGROUND TO THE STORY
WHAT’s GOING ON
In Yemen, the Iran-aligned Houthis, who control much of Yemen, have been attacking ships passing through the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea for weeks in what they say is a response to Israel's war in Gaza.

But they are also seizing the opportunity to bolster their popularity in Yemen. After a decade of conflict, Yemenis are experiencing profound economic and humanitarian crises, and the Houthis are struggling to provide basic services. These attacks shift the attention away from domestic challenges and allow the Houthis to depict themselves as being on the frontlines of a regional war against Israel and the United States, in defense of the Palestinian cause. Finally, the Houthis lack legitimacy on the global stage; the Yemen-based group is trying to attract international attention and demonstrate that larger actors cannot simply ignore them.

THE SPIN OFF HITTING THE SHIPPING INDUSTRY
The hostilities have put a chokehold on ship passages through the Suez Canal, which handles about 12% of worldwide trade. The Suez Canal is most vital to the movement of goods between Asia and Europe, but global logistics executives warned that sending ships on alternate routes could roil global supply chains, causing backups at ports and shortages of vessels, containers and equipment that are suddenly in the wrong place. It is an extraordinary detour: Hundreds of ships are avoiding the Suez Canal and sailing an extra
4,000 miles around Africa, burning fuel, inflating costs and adding 10 days of travel or more in each direction.


WHY DO WE CARE
These ships are literally sailing past South Africa and stopping in Mozambique or Namib to refuel and restock. The country is losing out.

And consumers will be paying for it in the long run with increased logistics costs. Shipping companies have tripled the prices they charge to take a container from Asia to Europe, partly to cover the extra cost of sailing around Africa. Shipowners that still use the Red Sea, mainly tanker owners, face rising insurance premiums.

WHY AREN’t THEY STOPPING?
The South African Revenue Services (SARS) banned Off Port Limits (OPL) marine bunkering services earlier this year, meaning that vessels can no longer refuel and maintain their vessels outside port limits.

The temporary bunkering ban was placed shortly after five vessels, including four bunker tankers and one oil drilling ship, were impounded in Algoa Bay by SARS amid an ongoing investigation into the alleged violation of tax rules in September. The bunker tankers, connected to Minerva Bunkering
Marine Services and TFG Marine, were anchored in Algoa Bay, while the drilling ship was anchored in the port of Ngqura.

Experts say the moratorium was an ill-advised decision; a significant misstep hampered South Africa’s golden opportunity in the maritime sector. This blockade, amid a global shipping crisis caused by the Red Sea route disruption, is short-sighted and economically damaging.

THE CURRENT STATE OF SA PORTs
South Africa’s major ports, including Durban, one of Africa’s largest in terms of container volumes handled, as well as Cape Town and Ngqura ports are among the WORST PERFORMING PORTS GLOBALLY - Yes - the WORST!!

The country’s ports have faced congestion in recent months, with Transnet aiming to clear the backlog at the Durban port in February 2023. The Durban port and Port Elizabeth are now among the top 30 most congested ports in the world, according to global shipping data.

ADD ON - OIL PRICES
This is the scenario now unfolding; it will come into sharper focus as time goes by and as a clearer picture of the war emerges.
At this point, risk vigilance must be intensified and responses drafted. South Africa and its business community must prepare for the worst.

ADDITIONAL INTERNATIONS COMMENTARY
THE CENTRE FOR STRATEGIC AND INTERNATIONAL STUDIES
Q: What are the macroeconomic consequences of the conflict?
A: The Red Sea crisis is directly responsible for cargo shipping delays and price increases in the short term. While the attacks on vessels are tied to the ever-changing conflict in the Middle East—and therefore difficult to predict in the medium to long term—delays and cost increases are highly likely to continue into the following months as shipping firms begin to plan for a protracted conflict. According to International Monetary Fund data as of January 22, 2024, the seven-day rolling average of Bab al-Mandab passages has dropped to 46 percent compared to the same period last year. Suez
Canal passages are at 63 percent compared to the previous year, while Cape of Good Hopepassages are up 70 percent. The increase in ship diversions increases fuel and labor costs while decreasing the average amount of cargo traffic reaching its destination. Egypt’s Suez Canal revenues have taken a hit due to ship diversions. As of January 12, 2024, revenues are down 40 percent in comparison to 2023 levels. Worse yet for the Egyptian economy, canal fees are paid in foreign currency, which the government has struggled to obtain due to rapidly growing inflation.
Diversions and subsequent price increases affect different shipping industries in different ways. Bulk carriers, which carry less valuable cargo (often raw materials), are not impacted in the same way as cargo ships, which tend to transport more valuable goods. The Baltic Dry Index, which tracks the cost of transporting various raw materials provides insight into the macroeconomic impact of shipping delays. While the index spiked to above $3,000 in early to mid-December, the cost of shipping has dropped to $1,503 as of January 22, which is an approximately normal level. On the other hand, cargo shipping, which transports more value than bulk carriers (thus, is more likely to avoid the Red Sea) has had a sustained price increase. Drewry’s World Container Index—which tracks the average price of transporting a 40-foot (ft) container on a cargo ship— jumped from $1,521/40 ft on December 14, 2023, to $3,777/40 ft as of January 18, 2024. Routes from Asia to Europe, which normally transit the Red Sea, have seen the steepest increase in price. Drewry shows that the average Shanghai to Genoa shipment is above $6,000/40 ft. However, knock-on effects can be seen in unaffected routes. Shanghai to Los Angeles cargo rates jumped from $1,985/40 ft to $3,860/40 ft between December 14, 2023, and January 18, 2024. While these numbers suggest immediate increases in prices, other economic elements will factor into the cost of shipping in the long run. According to the Financial Times, carrier companies have ramped up their purchasing of vessels. Between 2022 and 2025, the global capacity of container shipping is expected to increase by around 25 percent, helping to control prices.

INTERNATIONAL NEWS CLIPS UPSOUND: “South Africa says this is evidence of genocide. Israel says this that’s an outrageous accusation”.
UPSOUND EXPLOSION

VO: Now, a new frontline emerges.

UPSOUND HOUTHI VIDEO - chopper landing on ship, men with weapons on deck

VO: Out at sea in the Middle East, ships are boarded in scenes you'd expect in a movie.

UPSOUND HOUTHI VIDEO - men with weapons on deck

VO: These are Yemen’s Houthi Rebels, attacking a British owned commercial cargo ship in the Red Sea

UPSOUND HOUTHI VIDEO - man shouting below deck with gun

VO: The Houthis say they’re acting in solidarity with Palestine. Since November there’s been 30 attacks.
TODMAN: they are trying to put pressure on the global economy in order to encourage Western states, in particular to force Israel to accept a cease fire in Gaza.
VO 10: Will Todman is from the Washington-based Middle East Programme at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies.
TODMAN: these attacks have really demonstrated the vulnerability of this chokepoints and of global maritime shipping. //ultimately, they're trying to // dissuade shipping companies from from transiting that area.

VO: And it’s working. With reported backing from Iran, the Houthi Rebels are targeting commercial shipping vessels in the Red Sea, a strategic global trade route.

LINK: The Middle East crisis presents danger, but also opportunity.

VO: Over one trillion US dollars in exports, flows through Egypt's Suez Canal trade route to Western markets every year. But hostilities in the Red Sea are putting a stop to it.
Cargo traffic in the region has dropped dramatically - as some major shipping companies opt for the longer transit route around the Cape of Good Hope sending supply chain costs soaring.
LINK: What you need to capitalize on that is preparedness, unfortunately, at our ports that's exactly what South Africa is missing.
VO: This man is a high ranking employee at Transnet, the State-run company in charge of our ports and harbours. He asked not to be identified.

INSIDER: We are in a dire status.
GOVAN: Do you think Transnet and South African ports could cope with increased shipping traffic.
INSIDER: If Transnet was managed very well, it would cope. But the problem is that Transnet is not managed very well.

VO: South Africa’s major harbours ranked are amongst the worst performing container ports globally - with Durban and Port Elizabeth in the top 30 most congested ports.

INSIDER: The problem is the leadership and the inefficiency of servicing port users is the one that is a problem in Transnet space. Creating problems in our South African ports.

VO: And, problems in the economy - We're missing out on valuable foreign money, valuable revenue for a stagnant economy

In November 2023 the Port of Durban hit a major crisis - almost 80 vessels and more than 61,000 containers were stuck in the ocean unable to dock. The reason? Operational challenges, equipment failures, and bad weather.

Rosario Sarno is the Managing Director of the Mediterranean Shipping Company - one of the world’s largest.

ROSARIO: It was a big crisis. It was expected, to be honest. We knew that the equipment was old. We knew that the situation had to be rectified//
**
VO: It's a crisis a long time in the making - Transnet's been costing the economy for a while.

Moshe Motlohi is from Transnet’s National Ports Authority.

FINAL MIX FIX STUDIO
GOVAN: Transnet's own reports showing that it lost MILLIONS OF RANDSdue to inefficiency ?
MOSHE: Yes. No, you're right. // We haNdLED less ships. // because of inefficiency. Of course, the EARNINGS were reduced //.
GOVAN: But that's money lost. That's money in the water. And it can never recover.
MOSHE: Definitely.
GOVAN: So do you admit it’s an inefficient port?
MOSHE: What then do we do? Do we sit down and say it is inefficient and do nothing? We recovered.

VO: But that recovery hasn't been enough to capitalise on the increased shipping traffic fleeing from Houthi attacks. HUNDREDS of commercial cargo ships have not stopped at our ports and are merely passing by the South African coastline.

LINK: The best way to capitalize on the diverted ships is to offer them refuelling and restocking. That's called bunkering.

VO: Think of it as floating petrol stations servicing the passing ships at sea.

Unathi Sonti is from the Maritime Business Chamber.?

BOAT UNATHI: // vessels are able to get, you know, fuel without going inside the port. And you get all the services that you require and then you continue with your voyage.
GOVAN: Seeing this ship Up close like this. It really puts it into perspective that this thing can make a lot of money. // Is that of Benefit to South Africa?
UNATHI: we're not benefiting. // It’s a missed and wasted opportunity

VO: Shipping companies are heading to our neighbouring countries - as our refuelling limitations cripple an industry worth billions of rands.

LINK: This ship and four others have been sitting idle since September last year. They've been seized while SARS is figuring out how to tax the fuel they supply to passing ships.

BOAT UNATI: they are detained to be here. They can’t move. They can't do anything. They can't do any work. And they can leave the South African waters up until SARS finishes what they call is the investigation

VO: While SARS hasn’t figured out how to tax existing off-shore bunkering companies. Government is also not allowing any new licences. This means, this lucrative service - if controversial - is now at a complete standstill.

GOVAN: Do you think that's a missed opportunity for South Africa?
ROSARIO: Yes, of course. We have bigger problems than the bunkering at this stage. // we have to fix other things do have the priority.

VO: Most South African Ports are struggling to meet international demand irrespective of the Middle East crisis ship traffic.

The backlogs in Durban are a prime example. But to get a better perspective we're taking to the sky with local chopper pilot Ash Badul.

UPSOUND
TAKE OFF RADIO CHATTER
ASH: copy that.
GOVAN UP SOUND - TIME TO TAKE OFF

LINK: We’re only allowed to fly on the white water. That means//we can’t get too close to the ships which are anchored out sea

ASH: I often fly along the coastline.
GOVAN: Is it normal to see that many of them?
ASH: Not until recently, I once counted 40 vessels.
GOVAN: 40 ships!
ASH: There were more ships in the ocean than fish.

LINK: It’s a magnificent sight, the largest port in Sub-saharan Africa, and the busiest too, but what makes it inefficient is the time it takes to process the ships, there are over a dozen still waiting out at sea – and that’s the problem.

VO: AND sitting outside the port, is costly.

ROSARIO: //Waiting time is probably around 12 days. The cost of one of those vessels is probably around $50,000 per day. // it's like a half a million dollars that is going out due to these delays.

VO: But that’s money in the water for everyone.

INSIDER: Transnet itself is losing money // you are failing to deliver on what is expected of you from customers. That reflects the failure of managing the port system

GOVAN: Does it make South African ports unattractive to international shipping companies?
ROSARIO: Yes, 100% - but this is a big fear that big companies will not come to South Africa any more. That is not entirely true.

ADD A BEAT - OF HARBOUR SHOT

LINK: The reality is that South Africa's ports are way too strategic to give up on. International shipping companies need us.

A BEAT OF 2 seconds to get from link to question….

VO: But they also can’t afford to carry costs that should be avoidable.

GOVAN: Anchorage time of 7 to 12 days is unacceptable InternationalLY
MOSHE: It is unacceptable. // I want us to be clear, // THERE ARE terminals here that are world class, they do not have those delays. / We should isolate the problem areas. But we have seen the improvement

VO: But the ports still have a long way to go - especially in the Durban container terminals.

ROSARIO: We’re probably doing 12 / 13 containers, per crane. It should be around 20 and plus. For the last four years, there hasn't been any investment.

GOVAN: The criticism is that there's been a systematic degradation of transnet's ability to service vessels at the ports because it hasn't been buying the equipment that's necessary.
MOSHE: //of course they are correct // not, because people did not know what they needed to do. It's just that that investment did not come.

VO: Motlohi assures us investment and maintenance are now a priority. But it’s too soon to celebrate - with some orders taking up to 18 months for delivery..

MOSHE: The situation is going to improve, not because we are saying so, but because we are doing something. // We have people that can step in and keep the economy moving // -

VO: With a recent management shake up at Transnet - shipping operators like Sarno are choosing to be optimistic.

ROSARIO: we are stabilizing the ship. And I'm quite sure that in the very near future we'll be going full steam ahead again.// There is a political will to succeed. It cannot fail.

VO: Especially when golden opportunities to boost South Africa’s fragile economy, are passing by our shores.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): DISRUPTIONS IN WORLD TRADE triggered by war create a golden opportunity for South Africa to boost its own economy - but ironically it’s an opportunity the country is missing out on. SUMMARY
metadata.Unique Selling Point: A WAR STORY WITHOUT IT BEING ABOUT WAR
metadata.Summary: In any war there is collateral damage, direct and indirect economic impact and ironically even opportunities for some to benefit. Right now, global trade is being disrupted as attacks in the Red Sea hots up, with shipping companies vowing to avoid those waters rerouting ships thousands of miles away around the Cape of Good Hope. It could be a golden opportunity for South Africa - but it’s not. We ask why.
metadata.Further information: WHY TELL THIS STORY? This is a way to do a story about the war, without doing a story about war and making relevant to South Africa HOW WE TELL THIS STORY We set the scene - the war in Gaza, the attacks in Yemen using visuals of the attacks. Then we demonstrate the ripple effect on the shipping industry using maps and graphics. This is our springboard into looking at the current crisis at South African ports and the red tape that’s causing the country to lose out on potentially very lucrative opportunity to benefit from war. We take it up a notch by including transnet / shipping industry insider that will act a as a deep throat - explaining the shortcomings of a port system broken by ineffective management, a lack of resources and of course corruption (dealt with in broad strokes - no crazy RORs) BACKGROUND TO THE STORY WHAT’s GOING ON In Yemen, the Iran-aligned Houthis, who control much of Yemen, have been attacking ships passing through the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea for weeks in what they say is a response to Israel's war in Gaza. But they are also seizing the opportunity to bolster their popularity in Yemen. After a decade of conflict, Yemenis are experiencing profound economic and humanitarian crises, and the Houthis are struggling to provide basic services. These attacks shift the attention away from domestic challenges and allow the Houthis to depict themselves as being on the frontlines of a regional war against Israel and the United States, in defense of the Palestinian cause. Finally, the Houthis lack legitimacy on the global stage; the Yemen-based group is trying to attract international attention and demonstrate that larger actors cannot simply ignore them. THE SPIN OFF HITTING THE SHIPPING INDUSTRY The hostilities have put a chokehold on ship passages through the Suez Canal, which handles about 12% of worldwide trade. The Suez Canal is most vital to the movement of goods between Asia and Europe, but global logistics executives warned that sending ships on alternate routes could roil global supply chains, causing backups at ports and shortages of vessels, containers and equipment that are suddenly in the wrong place. It is an extraordinary detour: Hundreds of ships are avoiding the Suez Canal and sailing an extra 4,000 miles around Africa, burning fuel, inflating costs and adding 10 days of travel or more in each direction. WHY DO WE CARE These ships are literally sailing past South Africa and stopping in Mozambique or Namib to refuel and restock. The country is losing out. And consumers will be paying for it in the long run with increased logistics costs. Shipping companies have tripled the prices they charge to take a container from Asia to Europe, partly to cover the extra cost of sailing around Africa. Shipowners that still use the Red Sea, mainly tanker owners, face rising insurance premiums. WHY AREN’t THEY STOPPING? The South African Revenue Services (SARS) banned Off Port Limits (OPL) marine bunkering services earlier this year, meaning that vessels can no longer refuel and maintain their vessels outside port limits. The temporary bunkering ban was placed shortly after five vessels, including four bunker tankers and one oil drilling ship, were impounded in Algoa Bay by SARS amid an ongoing investigation into the alleged violation of tax rules in September. The bunker tankers, connected to Minerva Bunkering Marine Services and TFG Marine, were anchored in Algoa Bay, while the drilling ship was anchored in the port of Ngqura. Experts say the moratorium was an ill-advised decision; a significant misstep hampered South Africa’s golden opportunity in the maritime sector. This blockade, amid a global shipping crisis caused by the Red Sea route disruption, is short-sighted and economically damaging. THE CURRENT STATE OF SA PORTs South Africa’s major ports, including Durban, one of Africa’s largest in terms of container volumes handled, as well as Cape Town and Ngqura ports are among the WORST PERFORMING PORTS GLOBALLY - Yes - the WORST!! The country’s ports have faced congestion in recent months, with Transnet aiming to clear the backlog at the Durban port in February 2023. The Durban port and Port Elizabeth are now among the top 30 most congested ports in the world, according to global shipping data. ADD ON - OIL PRICES This is the scenario now unfolding; it will come into sharper focus as time goes by and as a clearer picture of the war emerges. At this point, risk vigilance must be intensified and responses drafted. South Africa and its business community must prepare for the worst. ADDITIONAL INTERNATIONS COMMENTARY THE CENTRE FOR STRATEGIC AND INTERNATIONAL STUDIES Q: What are the macroeconomic consequences of the conflict? A: The Red Sea crisis is directly responsible for cargo shipping delays and price increases in the short term. While the attacks on vessels are tied to the ever-changing conflict in the Middle East—and therefore difficult to predict in the medium to long term—delays and cost increases are highly likely to continue into the following months as shipping firms begin to plan for a protracted conflict. According to International Monetary Fund data as of January 22, 2024, the seven-day rolling average of Bab al-Mandab passages has dropped to 46 percent compared to the same period last year. Suez Canal passages are at 63 percent compared to the previous year, while Cape of Good Hopepassages are up 70 percent. The increase in ship diversions increases fuel and labor costs while decreasing the average amount of cargo traffic reaching its destination. Egypt’s Suez Canal revenues have taken a hit due to ship diversions. As of January 12, 2024, revenues are down 40 percent in comparison to 2023 levels. Worse yet for the Egyptian economy, canal fees are paid in foreign currency, which the government has struggled to obtain due to rapidly growing inflation. Diversions and subsequent price increases affect different shipping industries in different ways. Bulk carriers, which carry less valuable cargo (often raw materials), are not impacted in the same way as cargo ships, which tend to transport more valuable goods. The Baltic Dry Index, which tracks the cost of transporting various raw materials provides insight into the macroeconomic impact of shipping delays. While the index spiked to above $3,000 in early to mid-December, the cost of shipping has dropped to $1,503 as of January 22, which is an approximately normal level. On the other hand, cargo shipping, which transports more value than bulk carriers (thus, is more likely to avoid the Red Sea) has had a sustained price increase. Drewry’s World Container Index—which tracks the average price of transporting a 40-foot (ft) container on a cargo ship— jumped from $1,521/40 ft on December 14, 2023, to $3,777/40 ft as of January 18, 2024. Routes from Asia to Europe, which normally transit the Red Sea, have seen the steepest increase in price. Drewry shows that the average Shanghai to Genoa shipment is above $6,000/40 ft. However, knock-on effects can be seen in unaffected routes. Shanghai to Los Angeles cargo rates jumped from $1,985/40 ft to $3,860/40 ft between December 14, 2023, and January 18, 2024. While these numbers suggest immediate increases in prices, other economic elements will factor into the cost of shipping in the long run. According to the Financial Times, carrier companies have ramped up their purchasing of vessels. Between 2022 and 2025, the global capacity of container shipping is expected to increase by around 25 percent, helping to control prices.
